1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation has converged on the polarity-duration signature of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Core pathophysiology remains stable: outer hair cell / cochlear function preserved → OAEs present, cochlear microphonic CM present; inner hair cell–auditory nerve synapse / neural synchrony impaired → compound neural ABR absent or severely dys-synchronous, typically absent/non-reproducible Waves III-V at up to 95 dB nHL, often with intermittent Wave I. CM is pre-neural, stimulus-locked, polarity sensitive and inverts with stimulus polarity. True neural ABR is essentially polarity insensitive and first develops after ~1 ms post click; in normal hearing condensation and rarefaction ABRs superimpose after polarity inversion for the neural window, with only the very early ≤~1 ms CM portion showing polarity reversal.

Polarity test dissociates preserved CM from absent neural synchrony.

Round 3 public positions are now unanimous for D. Colleagues 1-15 all give D. Earlier minority for C from round 0, Colleagues 2 and 8, has shifted. Earlier dispute about wording of C – persistence of mirroring >1 ms because the neural polarity-invariant component is absent – is now resolved in favour of the physiological description: the polarity-sensitive generator itself is the brief CM limited to ≤1 ms. The loss of the neural ABR beyond ~1 ms is seen clinically as absence/non-reproducibility of Waves III-V, not as a sustained physiologic polarity-reversing potential persisting into the 2-6 ms window. Colleagues who previously argued for C now explicitly reject the >1 ms sustained mirror claim as a misreading of absent neural activity for continued polarity sensitivity.

Shared reasoning now: in ANSD the only stimulus-locked activity that can be averaged is the preserved polarity-sensitive CM / stimulus artefact. Condensation and rarefaction averaged waveforms are mirror images of each other only while CM dominates, i.e. for the brief early receptor-potential window conventionally ≤~0.5-1 ms post onset. No reproducible polarity-invariant Waves I-III-V develop thereafter; beyond ~1 ms the record is absent / noise / non-replicable, the classic picture of present OAEs/CM with absent/non-reproducible ABR at 95 dB nHL, often intermittent Wave I and absent/distorted III-V.

A – peaks 1 and 3 present, peak 5 absent – and B – prolonged latencies of peaks 1 and 3 at 95 dBnHL – are rejected as not the defining polarity sign; A describes selective peak loss, B describes retrocochlear conduction delay.

Unresolved nuance remains only rhetorical: operational descriptions of “no polarity invariance beyond ~1 ms” can be phrased as abnormal mirroring persisting >1 ms in the sense that the normal break in mirroring does not occur. The consensus wording used in the answer options is D: wave pattern in condensation is a mirror image of the wave pattern in rarefaction for a duration of ≤1 ms.

Current belief: D is correct.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: D

Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder is the dissociation of a preserved cochlear receptor potential/OAE/cochlear microphonic system from loss of phase-locked inner hair cell–auditory nerve synchrony. OAEs and the cochlear microphonic are typically present/normal whereas the compound neural ABR I-III-V is absent, severely dys-synchronous or non-reproducible even at 95 dB nHL, often with at best an intermittent low-latency Wave I and absent/distorted/non-reproducible Waves III-V.

The cochlear microphonic is a pre-neural receptor potential that follows the fine structure of the stimulus and is therefore polarity sensitive. Condensation and rarefaction clicks evoke mirror-image CMs. The CM is stimulus-locked and essentially co-temporal with the click, confined to the very early onset window conventionally ≈ ≤0.5–1 ms post stimulus.

A true neurogenic ABR is essentially polarity insensitive / onset locked and normally first appears > ~1 ms as Waves I-III-V. In normal hearing the <~1 ms portion is CM dominated and polarity reversing, after ~1 ms the polarity invariant neural ABR dominates so condensation and rarefaction traces superimpose after polarity correction.

In ANSD neural phase locking is lost. The only stimulus-locked activity that can be averaged is the preserved polarity-sensitive cochlear microphonic / stimulus artefact. Hence condensation and rarefaction averaged waveforms remain mirror images of each other only while the CM dominates, i.e. for the brief early receptor-potential window conventionally ≤ ~1 ms post onset, and no reproducible polarity-invariant Waves I-III-V develop thereafter. Beyond ~1 ms the record is essentially absent/noise/non-replicable; that is loss of the normal neural ABR, not a sustained physiological polarity-reversing potential.

A is a selective peak loss pattern and B is latency prolongation, not the defining polarity sign. The classic ABR polarity signature of ANSD is therefore a brief early ≤1 ms polarity-reversing mirror image due to preserved CM with loss of the normal polarity-invariant neural waveform beyond ~1 ms, with present OAEs/CM and an absent/non-reproducible ABR at high intensity.
